questions.q: What are the three stages of the RLHF pipeline, in order?
options: Reward model training, then PPO, then SFT
Supervised fine-tuning (SFT), then reward model training, then PPO fine-tuning against the reward model
PPO, then SFT, then reward model training
SFT, then PPO, then reward model training
questions.explain: RLHF is a fixed three-stage pipeline: SFT produces a starting policy, a reward model is trained on preference comparisons of that policy's outputs, and PPO then fine-tunes the SFT policy against the reward model.

questions.q: Why is the reward model trained on comparisons between responses sampled from the SFT model specifically, rather than from the raw pretrained base model?
options: It makes no difference which model generated the sampled responses
Because the reward model's preference judgments need to be calibrated to the response distribution PPO will actually be sampling from during RL, which is the SFT model's distribution
Because the pretrained base model cannot generate any text at all
Because reward models can only be trained on a single response per prompt
questions.explain: If the reward model were trained on comparisons from a different (weaker) policy's outputs, its judgments would be miscalibrated for the distribution of text PPO generates during RL fine-tuning.

questions.q: Why does PPO fine-tuning start from the SFT checkpoint instead of the raw pretrained base model?
options: Starting from the SFT checkpoint avoids spending RL steps teaching the model basic instruction-following on a noisy, indirect reward signal
The pretrained base model cannot be loaded into a PPO trainer
Starting from SFT is required by the Bradley-Terry objective
It has no effect on training efficiency either way
questions.explain: The SFT model already follows instructions reasonably well, so RL fine-tuning can focus on refining behavior rather than learning it from scratch under a much noisier reward signal.

questions.q: In this pipeline, what role does the frozen reference model play, and where does it come from?
options: It is a randomly initialized model used only for debugging
It is a copy of the SFT checkpoint, kept unchanged throughout RL, used to measure how far the policy has drifted
It is the reward model itself, renamed
It is the pretrained base model, used to replace the policy if PPO fails
questions.explain: The reference model is a frozen copy of the SFT checkpoint; the policy is compared against it (via the KL penalty, covered next lesson) to catch drift during RL fine-tuning.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what changes about PPO's clipped objective, GAE, or the reward model's Bradley-Terry training when they're used inside the RLHF pipeline?
options: Nothing about those mechanics changes; what's new is that PPO's reward function becomes a call to the trained reward model on generated text
PPO's clipping range must be set to zero inside RLHF
The Bradley-Terry objective is replaced by a different loss function
GAE can no longer be used once a reward model is introduced
questions.explain: PPO's objective, advantage estimation, and the reward model's training objective all carry over unchanged from earlier chapters; the new element is that the reward signal PPO optimizes now comes from the trained reward model instead of a hand-written environment reward.
